items.title: Data protection basics for public bodies
items.source: UK GDPR; Data Protection Act 2018; Information Commissioner's Office guidance
items.body: The UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 set the rules for personal data, and the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) regulates them. Every use of personal data needs a lawful basis. Public authorities most often rely on public task, meaning the processing is necessary to carry out their official functions; consent is rarely suitable where people have no real choice. A data protection impact assessment (DPIA) is required before processing that is likely to result in high risk to people, such as large-scale use of sensitive data, systematic monitoring or new technology. The assessment describes the purpose, tests necessity, identifies risks to people and sets out how they will be reduced, with advice from the data protection officer.

questions.prompt: Which body regulates data protection in the UK?
Which lawful basis do public authorities most often rely on for their core work?

options.text: Before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to individuals
Only when a supplier asks for one

questions.prompt: A new case-management system will bring together health and benefits data held by two teams. It is not yet bought. What data protection steps do you take?
questions.answer: Start a DPIA before procurement. Define the purpose and lawful basis, check the data is necessary and minimised, agree a data sharing arrangement between the teams, build in security and retention limits, update the privacy notice and take advice from the data protection officer. If a high residual risk remains, consult the ICO before processing.
questions.rubric: Should include early DPIA, purpose and lawful basis, minimisation, data sharing agreement, security and retention, privacy notice, DPO advice, ICO consultation if high residual risk.

items.title: Privacy notices and individual rights
items.source: UK GDPR; Data Protection Act 2018; Information Commissioner's Office guidance
items.body: A privacy notice tells people what data is held, why, the lawful basis, who it is shared with, how long it is kept and what rights they have, in plain language and at the time the data is collected. People have rights over their data, including to see it. A subject access request must be answered within one month, which can be extended by up to two further months for complex requests. The team verifies identity, searches all relevant systems, removes or redacts information about other people unless it is reasonable to disclose it, applies any exemptions and explains what has been provided. Some rights are not absolute: the right to erasure, for example, does not apply where the data must be kept to meet a legal obligation or to perform a public task.

questions.prompt: What should a privacy notice explain?

options.text: Only the name of the organisation
Only the cost of the service
What data is held, why, how long, who it is shared with and the person's rights

questions.prompt: What is the normal time limit for answering a subject access request?
Can a person always insist that a public body deletes their records?

options.text: No, the right to erasure has limits such as legal obligations and public tasks
Only if the records are paper

questions.prompt: A resident has sent a subject access request. Their records are in three different teams' systems and include letters naming other people. How do you handle it?
questions.answer: Log the date received and confirm identity, then ask each team to search and return what they hold. Review the records, redact or withhold information about other people unless disclosure is reasonable, apply any relevant exemptions and give the person a copy with the required explanation within one month, or extend and tell them if the request is complex.
questions.rubric: Should mention logging and ID check, searching all systems, redacting third-party data, exemptions, explanation and copy, one month limit with possible extension.

items.title: Freedom of Information
items.source: Freedom of Information Act 2000; Information Commissioner's Office guidance
items.body: The Freedom of Information Act 2000 gives anyone the right to ask a public authority for recorded information it holds. A request must be in writing, give the requester's name and an address for reply, and describe the information wanted. The authority must normally respond within 20 working days, either supplying the information or explaining which exemption applies. Some exemptions are absolute. Others are qualified, which means the information is withheld only if the public interest in doing so outweighs the public interest in disclosure. If answering would cost more than the appropriate limit in staff time, the authority may refuse, but must offer advice and assistance to help the requester narrow the request.

questions.prompt: How long does a public authority normally have to respond to an FOI request?
What does a valid FOI request need?

options.text: A reason for wanting the information
To be made on an official form
To be sent by recorded delivery
To be in writing, with the requester's name and an address for reply, describing the information wanted
One that applies only if the public interest in withholding outweighs the public interest in disclosure
One that only a qualified lawyer may use
One that applies to all personal data

questions.prompt: Someone asks for every email that mentions a particular supplier over five years. You estimate it would take far more than the cost limit. What do you do?
questions.answer: Explain that complying would exceed the cost limit and can be refused on that ground, but help the person narrow the request, for example by time period, team or subject, and invite a revised request. Keep a record of the search estimate and tell them about the internal review and the right to complain to the ICO.
questions.rubric: Should say the request can be refused for exceeding the cost limit, but the authority must advise and assist to narrow it, explain the estimate, and mention internal review and ICO.

items.title: Records, data sharing and open data
items.source: Public Records Act 1958; Data Sharing Code of Practice; Open Government Licence
items.body: A retention schedule says how long each type of record is kept and what happens at the end: review, destruction or transfer to an archive. Keeping personal data longer than needed is itself a breach, and deleting records early may break the law. When two organisations share personal data, a data sharing agreement sets out what is shared, why, the legal basis, who is responsible for it, how it is protected and when it is deleted. Data that carries no personal or sensitive content can be published as open data in machine-readable formats, usually under the Open Government Licence, so others can reuse it. When a service closes, its data is sorted into what must be kept, what must be transferred and what must be securely deleted.

questions.prompt: What does a retention schedule record?

options.text: Who has access to the office
How long each type of record is kept and what happens to it afterwards

questions.prompt: What does a data sharing agreement set out?

options.text: Only the names of the signatories
What is shared, why, on what legal basis, who is responsible and how it is protected
Only the date of the first meeting

questions.prompt: Which licence do UK public bodies commonly use to publish open data?

options.text: A commercial licence for each user

questions.prompt: You are closing a service with eight years of case data in an old system. How do you plan what to do with the data?
questions.answer: Check the retention schedule and legal duties, decide which records must be kept or transferred (including to an archive where the law requires), securely delete the rest and get confirmation, keep enough metadata to answer information requests, brief the data protection officer and record every decision.
questions.rubric: Should include checking retention schedule and legal duties, keep/transfer/delete categories, secure deletion with evidence, answering information requests, DPO involvement and documentation.
